tax-planning.q: How does good tax planning save on pension savings?
tax-planning.a: Good tax planning means using the tax benefits on pension, provident and study-fund deposits, claiming the tax credits you are entitled to, and choosing savings products with favourable tax treatment. Pension deposits earn a significant tax benefit up to an annual ceiling, and drawing the money as an annuity earns a further one. Good planning can save tens of thousands of shekels a year.
amendment-190.q: What is Amendment 190, and how does it save on management fees and premiums?
amendment-190.a: Amendment 190 to the Supervision of Financial Services Law allows money to move between executive insurance policies and pension products while lowering management fees and premiums. By negotiating with the institutional body, the costs of pension savings can be cut significantly and long-term returns improved.
marginal-tax.q: What is the marginal tax rate, and how does it affect my savings?
marginal-tax.a: Your marginal tax rate is the percentage you pay on each additional shekel you earn. The higher your income, the higher the marginal rate. Pension deposits earn a tax credit at your marginal rate — so the higher your marginal rate, the bigger the benefit. For employees with a high marginal rate, pension deposits are one of the most effective ways to save tax.
severance-lump-or-annuity.q: Should severance pay be withdrawn as a lump sum or as an annuity?
severance-lump-or-annuity.a: Drawing severance pay as an annuity (from age 60) earns a significant tax benefit — an exemption of up to ₪8,880 a month (as of 2026), with the rest at a reduced rate. A lump-sum withdrawal is taxed at the regular rate. In most cases the annuity is better from a tax point of view — but the decision depends on your personal situation, your age and any immediate need for capital.
pension-tax-refund.q: How do I get a tax refund on pension deposits?
pension-tax-refund.a: Employees who pay into a pension through their employer receive the benefit automatically on their payslip. The self-employed, and employees who pay in privately, need to claim the tax credit in their annual return (yearly or every two years). A retroactive refund can be claimed for deposits that were not credited in the past — up to 6 years back.
pension-vs-gemel-vs-hishtalmut.q: What is the difference between a pension fund, a provident fund and a study fund?
pension-vs-gemel-vs-hishtalmut.a: A pension fund is long-term saving for retirement age and pays a monthly annuity. A provident fund (kupat gemel) is medium- to long-term saving that can be withdrawn as capital from age 60. A study fund (keren hishtalmut) is short- to medium-term saving (at least 6 years) with tax-free gains. Each product suits different savings goals.
lower-management-fees.q: How can management fees be lowered in pension, provident and study funds?
lower-management-fees.a: Management fees add up to tens of thousands of shekels over the years of saving. They can be lowered by negotiating with the institutional body — pension funds, provident funds and study funds — by moving the money to a body with lower fees, or by using Amendment 190. Even a difference of a single percentage point adds up to a significant sum over the years.
fees-in-every-product.q: Do management fees need checking outside the pension fund too?
fees-in-every-product.a: A difference of just one percentage point in management fees adds up to tens of thousands of shekels over the years. Ask each institutional body for an exact breakdown of the fees on your fund, your executive insurance and your study fund, and compare. In many cases the fee can be lowered through simple negotiation — even without switching funds.
fees-in-every-product.tip: Check the management fees on every product — not just the pension
improve-returns.q: How can returns in pension and provident funds be improved?
improve-returns.a: Better returns come from choosing investment tracks that suit your age and financial situation, lowering management fees, spreading your assets sensibly and keeping an eye on the fund's performance. Tailoring the investment track to you can add meaningful percentage points of return over time.
merge-funds.q: When is it worth consolidating pension and provident funds?
merge-funds.a: Consolidating is worth it when you have several funds with high management fees, when the portfolio is hard to keep track of, or when one fund can offer better terms. It cuts costs, makes the portfolio easier to manage and follow, and allows the investment track to be matched more precisely. That said, spreading money across funds is sometimes better — the decision depends on your personal circumstances.
child-savings.q: Savings for children — is it worth starting at birth?
child-savings.a: Absolutely. A small monthly deposit into a child's savings plan from two months old grows over 20+ years into a significant sum, thanks to compound interest. Choose a product with low management fees and good liquidity, and set the goal in advance (studies, a flat, building capital). The earlier you start, the longer the money works for you.
child-savings.tip: Savings for children — worth starting at birth
self-employed-pension.q: Self-employed? Don't put off your pension contributions
self-employed-pension.a: Self-employed people who put off deposits 'until business is better' lose significant tax benefits and years of growth that never come back. Start with a fixed monthly deposit, even a modest one, and increase it over time. Also make sure you have loss-of-working-capacity cover — without an employer behind you, it matters many times more.
self-employed-pension.tip: Self-employed? Don't put off your pension contributions
supplementary-health.q: Supplementary health insurance — is it worth it, and how do you avoid duplicate cover?
supplementary-health.a: Before buying supplementary health insurance, check what your health fund (kupat holim) and your existing pension already cover. Many people pay for overlapping cover without knowing it. The key is to fill the real gaps precisely — private surgery, expensive medicines, hospitalisation in a closed ward — rather than buying more policies across the board.
supplementary-health.tip: Supplementary health cover — not needless duplication
rights-fixing.q: What is fixing of rights, and why does it matter?
rights-fixing.a: Fixing of rights is a process in which the insured person fixes their medical entitlements in their health and life insurance, so that future changes in their health do not harm their cover. It matters because it guarantees full cover even if your health changes, and prevents claims being rejected because of a pre-existing medical condition.
disability-cover.a: Loss-of-working-capacity insurance is your first line of defence — no less important than the savings themselves. Make sure the amount of cover matches your current income, that the waiting period suits your financial means, and that the policy uses the 'objective occupation' definition. Many people discover only when they claim that their cover is narrow or irrelevant.
switch-agent.q: Can I move to you from a previous agent?
switch-agent.a: Certainly. Changing agent is a simple process that costs nothing and does not interrupt your cover. I handle the entire transfer and all the explanations with the institutional bodies.
life-changes.q: What happens when my family or work situation changes?
life-changes.a: Every change affects which cover is right. With every change — marriage, a birth, divorce, a new home or becoming self-employed — we sit down together and adapt the portfolio to the new reality.
first-meeting-cost.q: Does the first introductory meeting cost anything?
first-meeting-cost.a: The first introductory meeting is free of charge and without obligation. Its purpose is to understand your needs and suggest a clear direction — we only move forward together if you choose to.
independent-agent.q: Are you independent, or tied to a particular insurance company?
independent-agent.a: I am a financial planner and insurance agent, and I work with a range of insurance and pension companies to match a solution to your needs. As an agent I have ties to institutional bodies, and my activity is pension marketing, not objective pension advice.
lifelong-service.a: An annual portfolio review, updating your cover with every life change (marriage, a birth, a home, going self-employed), negotiating fees and terms with the companies, and close support when you claim — all under one roof.
claims-support.q: How does support work when making a claim?
claims-support.a: I take over managing the claim with the company — completing the documentation, following it up and acting on your behalf until the full cover is received. In most cases you won't have to make a single phone call.
remote-meetings.a: Yes. Meetings can be held at the office in Tel Aviv, on Zoom or by phone — whatever suits you. The guidance itself is the same in every format.
confidentiality.q: How is my information kept confidential?
confidentiality.a: All the information you provide is kept strictly confidential, subject to the Privacy Protection Law and the office's privacy policy. It is not passed to third parties without your consent.
annual-review.q: How often should the whole portfolio be reviewed?
annual-review.a: Family situation, workplace and health change — and with them, the right cover. It is worth setting an annual review meeting where we go through every product together: pension, provident fund, study fund and insurance. A routine update prevents costly gaps and allows costs to be lowered and returns improved.
annual-review.tip: One hour a year for a full portfolio review
